name: Palestinian Territories
summary_text: Trans visitors face a severe and divided risk environment. Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian territories, and the difference between them is decisive: consensual same-sex conduct is not an offence in the West Bank, while in Gaza the same conduct is punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment under a statute that has been enforced against LGBT people.  The West Bank operates under the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences against consensual private sexual conduct and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision criminalises consensual same-sex acts there. The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality, and Israel stopped applying the older Mandate criminal code in 1977.  Gaza is governed by Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936, which remains in force. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' with up to ten years' imprisonment, and the same code sets out broader historic terms, including sodomy with up to fourteen years and an 'act against the law of nature' with up to ten years. Section 152(1)(c), the only youth-linked provision cited, carries up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. The Human Rights Watch and the Human Dignity Trust hold the 1936 ordinance to be in force in Gaza; its applicability is contested by other commentators, and Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there.  No provision of either regime expressly prohibits trans identity, but the 1936 code's public-morality provisions are broad enough to catch trans people in practice. No legal gender recognition provisions are set out for the territories, and Equaldex reports no broad legal protections against discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people.  Formal legality does not describe what is encountered on the ground. Social and family persecution makes daily reality harsher than the written law, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are recorded. Palestinian police action against a planned event organised by al-Qaws drew a wave of hate messages that activists said posed a serious threat to the community, and rights groups condemned the police ban on LGBTQ activity. Palestinian Authority non-signatory status to key human rights treaties limits the protection machinery available to a visitor.  HIV prevention and care are inadequate. HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and epidemiological surveillance is lacking: only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered between 1988 and 2017, with the true figure believed to be far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, the collapse of the healthcare system together with Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.  Entry runs through Israel. Around 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence, and since June 2022 Israel has issued work permits to gay Palestinians granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence. LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers in Israel are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programmes and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation.

sources.title: Shaul Ganon / Aguda (Israeli-based gay rights group) - statement quoted in article
sources.documents: Arrest and torture of gay Palestinians by Palestinian Authority; PA practice of labeling gays as collaborators; two cases in last three years tried explicitly for being homosexuals; claim it became impossible to be an open gay in the PA since the intifada when police increasingly began enforcing Islamic law; claim gay Palestinians are blackmailed into working as informants by Israeli security services

name: Réunion
summary_text: Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France.  Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.  Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.  Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.  Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.  The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.

sources.title: French Penal Code, Article 225-1 as amended 18 November 2016
sources.documents: Criminal ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity; core legal protection applicable in Réunion as overseas department.
sources.detail: Cited as article 225-1 Code pénal; 1985 law for sexual orientation, July 2012 added 'sexual identity', 18 November 2016 law replaced with 'gender identity'
